gaps.note: EVERY POSITION ON THE FRONT FACE IS ESTIMATED. The only sources held are a three-quarter marketing render and photographs of a unit racked in service, and neither is orthographic. panel_measure refuses the photograph outright, and hand-anchoring it gives width- and height-derived scales that disagree far beyond its 3% gate - the RJ45 jacks read 11.5 mm against their known 15.8 because the right of the frame is further from the lens. So the ORDER of the face is evidence and the coordinates are not. Tracked as roc-ops/Portrayal#247.
gaps.wanted: a face-on photograph of the front with nothing plugged in, or a mechanical drawing from MaiaEdge. Either settles the whole face in one step.

gaps.note: IT IS A TOUCH SCREEN, and the vendor says so four times. The product documentation has NTP servers configurable "using the on-board web UI or the front panel's touch screen" and DNS "by navigating the menus on the front panel display on the front of your PBC"; the setup guide sets the management IP, gateway and netmask "using the touch screen on the front of the device", and reads the claim code "by navigating the menus on the touchscreen display (from the home screen display, tap on the Claim Info button)". v3 drew it as a blank grey plate, which left it out of the device's parts; it is placed now, as `display` in a `displays` group, so a parts list and a DCIM export both see it. Its 38 x 29 frame is an estimate from the rack photograph and the part says so.
gaps.wanted: a dimension for the display and its frame. WHAT it is has been settled, and it is now a part - maiaedge/pbc-2000-lcd@1 - rather than paint; only its SIZE is invented.

gaps.note: THREE DIFFERENT THINGS GLOW ON THIS FACE and two of them are modelled. The vendor's UI view draws a deliberate column of four round lamps immediately left of port 0, which the rack photograph could not show because the transceivers' pull tabs and their fibre cover that corner - those four are modelled, and WHAT EACH ONE MEANS is unknown, so they carry `for: chassis` rather than an invented identity. Each 100G port also carries ONE lamp (provenance `port-lamps`); its count is the maintainer's and NEITHER SOURCE SHOWS WHERE IT SITS, so it is drawn above the cage - the one place both sources rule out a four-lamp band - and that position is a guess. Separately the photograph shows red and green points scattered at irregular positions and heights across BOTH vent fields; those are internal board LEDs glowing through the louvres, not a panel array - they do not line up and they sit at several louvre heights - and they are deliberately not drawn. No document held carries an LED table for any of the three.
gaps.wanted: an LED table, or a photograph of the unit powered down so the louvres read clean.

gaps.note: common/psu-550w@2 is placed, being the maintained major and the 73.5 mm CRPS 1U standard width. The rear photograph disagrees: on the scale the five fans validate to 0.2%, the two-supply block reads about 171 mm, or 85.5 mm each, which is far closer to the RETIRED common/psu-550w@1 at 84.0. An attempt to confirm the module seams programmatically failed, so the reading rests on an eyeball and is not asserted here. Either MaiaEdge fits a wider-than-CRPS module, or the eyeball is wrong. THE SQUARER REAR PHOTOGRAPH (pbc-rear-b.jpeg, 4.556 px/mm) NOW READS IT TOO: the first supply's cage 19.3 to 102.1 mm, a 15 mm steel strip, and the second's 117.4 to 196.4 - 79 to 83 mm a supply, not 73.5. The second supply is placed at its measured cage, centred; the 73.5 part is still what is drawn, so bare steel shows either side of both supplies until the module is identified.
gaps.wanted: a face-on rear photograph, or the vendor's part number for the supply. The answer decides which of the library's two 550W majors this device should carry.

gaps.note: These four faces draw the chassis envelope and nothing else. The envelope itself is not a guess - 437.90 x 291.08 x 41.27 is dimensioned on page 3 of the datasheet - but no source held shows what is ON any of them: no vent field, no label, no screw pattern, no rail. The flat rect asserts the box and claims nothing about its surface, which is what lets the device carry a rack elevation and a 3D box without inventing detail.
gaps.wanted: photographs of the lid, the underside and either flank out of the rack. The unit was shot in service with a device directly above it.

gaps.note: The centre band carries the word MaiaEdge in the vendor's amber, sized and coloured to match the photograph. The LOGO MARK that sits immediately left of it - a stylised angular glyph - is not drawn. Approximating a company's mark from a perspective photograph would be drawing something nobody can check, and a wrong logo is worse than an absent one.
gaps.wanted: the MaiaEdge mark as vector art, or a face-on photograph square enough to trace it from.

gaps.note: The datasheet states the supply configuration and no chassis draw figure, so none is recorded. L27 stands, and the chassis total is a floor rather than a total.
gaps.wanted: a chassis draw or input figure from MaiaEdge.

a `power-draw-max-w` on each module this chassis accepts, from the vendor's own per-card table - Cisco publishes one per ambient, most vendors publish none, and until they land a module total is a floor

which optics actually run in each pluggable cage - as prose in `attrs.optics-<media>` for now, which at least reaches the group, and structurally once enough vendors are in to say what the vocabulary has to hold

`cpu`, `memory` in a missing `attrs.platform` section; one of `power-max-w`, `power-max-ac-w`, `power-max-dc-w` in `attrs.power`; one of `operating-temp`, `operating-temp-f2b`, `operating-temp-b2f` in `attrs.environmental` (profile `networking` - see spec/schemas/profiles.yaml) - unlocks the About panel, and comparison against other devices
`physical-context` on 1 bay (rear 1); `physical-context` on port groups furniture, qsfp28 - unlocks ENTITY-MIB / Redfish correlation and monitoring overlays
the Nautobot exporter is not importable - unlocks NetBox / Nautobot device-type export

bezel.note: ESTIMATED shape, from photographs and the maintainer's account of the hardware (2026-09-21). The front is a BUILT-IN BEZEL standing about 11 mm off the faceplate, from the left edge to the touch screen, with the two OCTAGONAL windows cut through it: the octagons frame the faceplate behind, where the ports are. It is flat only across the band level with the windows' vertical ends, and slopes back to the faceplate above and below. That plate is maiaedge/pbc-2000-bezel@1 and its own provenance carries the figures. v3 drew the slope as shading on a flat face; the window walls are the amber bead, which is what looking into a window shows. The right-hand end of the right window is the only window end unobstructed by cabling in any photograph held, and is what the chamfer was read from. `shape: octagon` was added to the format for this - decor and cutouts could draw a rectangle, a rounded rectangle, a D-sub shell and a stadium slot, and an octagon had no shape to be.

cutouts.note: registry - each opening is the APERTURE the component declares, not the component's outline: common/qsfp-cage@2 is 19.5 x 10.18 of metal around an 18.5 x 9.58 hole offset (0.575, 0.6) into it, and a USB-A is 17.0 x 9.3 around a 12.0 x 4.5 hole at (2.5, 2.4). The first draft punched the outlines and test_cutout_derivation caught all three.

jacks.note: L76 and docs/rj45-family-design.md settle which part each jack is: an Ethernet jack is common/rj45-eth@1 and a console or timing jack is std/rj45@2. CON is the console, so it is the std part; MGMT and CTRL are the two 1GB management ports the datasheet counts, so they are the Ethernet part. All three were std/rj45@2 in the first draft and the rule caught it. THE TWO ETHERNET JACKS ARE FITTED TAB UP and the console jack is not: the photograph reads MGMT's and CTRL's contacts along the bottom of the opening with the latch slot above, and CON's the other way about. Declared as rotate 180, because a jack fitted the other way up is the same jack turned over rather than a reflection of it, and its lamps really do change sides.

layout.note: ESTIMATED, AND THE WORD IS EXACT. The ORDER and GROUPING of everything on the front face are read off photographs of a unit in service (see gaps `front-positions`); the POSITIONS are a plausible arrangement consistent with them and with each component's own size. No position here is a measurement. The one position that is better than that is the chassis status lamp: the photograph puts it unambiguously in the notch outside the right window's lower-right chamfer, and it is placed against that edge rather than against a coordinate.

lint-l64.note: THREE L64 WARNINGS ON THIS DEVICE ARE THE RULE READING A LOUVRE AS AIR. The CON, MGMT and CTRL legends sit inside the right louvre field, which L64 reads as open end to end. On the hardware the louvres are slots in metal and the legends are printed on the bars between them. The legends are where the photograph shows them. Do not move them to quiet the rule. The bezel's windows no longer draw L44 or L21, and the two cages no longer draw L64: lint reads the windows from the bezel's `shape` relief, and punches a part through its cutout by its opening rather than its flange.

louvres.note: photo-measured (COUNT ONLY) - each window carries a grid of short horizontal slots, EIGHT ROWS DEEP AND FIVE COLUMNS ACROSS, counted on the rack photograph and confirmed by the maintainer against the hardware. One column of the left window, isolated and contrast-normalised, reads eight slots between the beads; the unobstructed band above the transceivers reads four ribs, so five columns. The PITCH IS NOT MEASURED: it is those counts divided into the window as modelled, and the window itself is estimated. What the count corrects is a shape, not a dimension - the marketing render draws the field as full-width louvres and the first draft copied it, so this face wore a texture the hardware does not have.

model-number.note: vendor documentation - www.maiaedge.io/getting-started (getting-started.pdf), Safety Information: "The PBC-2000 is equipped with two redundant AC power inputs." THE DATASHEET AND THE MANAGEMENT UI BOTH SAY ONLY "PBC", which is what this device was first modelled as; the setup guide is the only source held that gives the number. A DCIM reads `model` as the identity, so it is the number and not the family.

numbering.note: MaiaEdge's own management UI (working/intake/maiaedge/pbc/renders/ui-port-view.png) numbers the two 100G ports 0 and 1, so the group is index-origin 0, and captions them 100G. It captions MGMT and CTRL 1G and CON not at all, and - independently of L76 - DRAWS CON AS A DIFFERENT JACK from the other two, which is the console-versus- Ethernet split the rule had already forced. A UI view is a schematic: it is taken here for what is on the face, in what order, and what the vendor calls it. No coordinate comes from it.

port-lamps.note: field knowledge (the maintainer, 2026-09-15), corroborated NEGATIVELY by both sources held - ONE lamp per 100G port. The photograph shows the louvres running straight up to the cage flange with no lamp band above it, and the vendor's UI view draws each port with nothing above it either; neither shows where the one lamp sits, because the transceivers' pull tabs cover that corner. So the COUNT is the maintainer's and the POSITION is estimated. This is why the plain common/qsfp-cage@2 is fitted rather than common/qsfp28-cage@3, whose four lamps belong to the AS7726-32X's panel by its own provenance and are not a property of any cage.

ports.note: datasheet page 3 - "Dual 100GbE Ethernet (QSFP28)", "2x 1GB RJ45" management, "1x USB 2.0", "RJ45 115.2 kbps" console. Confirmed on the hardware: the front photograph reads the three jacks' own silkscreen as CON, MGMT and CTRL, which is the console plus the two management ports the table counts. AND NOW STATED BY THE VENDOR IN PROSE, which is better than either: the setup guide (www.maiaedge.io/getting-started) describes the face directly - the front has "two windows where the ports are exposed"; the lefthand window has "two 100G interfaces, numbered 0 and 1 from left to right"; and in the righthand window, "from left to right, you'll find a USB port (not currently used), a serial console port, a 10/100/1000 management port, and a 10/100/1000 control port". It calls MGMT "the PBC's center management port" and CTRL "rightmost port in the right window". Every one of those matches what was modelled from the photograph and the UI view; the ORDER of this face is no longer an inference. The vendor's own word for the octagonal cutouts is `window`, which is what the decor already calls them. Note the guide rates the two jacks 10/100/1000 where the table says 1GB, and calls the USB port NOT CURRENTLY USED.

power.note: datasheet page 3 - "Internal: AC, DC" with "Redundant Power Supply: Yes". The 550W per-supply figure is photo-measured: both modules carry a blue 550W label. The datasheet states no chassis draw, so none is recorded and L27 stands.

rear.note: photo-measured - working/intake/maiaedge/pbc/photos/pbc-rear-b.jpeg, the one rear shot square enough to scale: anchored on the 437.90 mm chassis width (x 210 to 2205 px, 4.556 px/mm) it reads the face 41.7 mm tall against the datasheet's 41.27, 1% out. On that scale the second supply's cage starts at 117.4 mm and the fan tray at 196.4. THE WHOLE REAR IS BARE STEEL, ear to ear, in both rear photographs; v3 left most of it the chassis's black. THE FIVE FANS ARE ONE TRAY, not five trays: one continuous plate with a thumbscrew at its left end, a field-replaceable unit (the maintainer, 2026-09-21). v3 drew five common/fan-module-41 trays with red pull tabs; maiaedge/pbc-2000-fan-plate@1 replaces them in one bay, which is why this is 4.0.0 - the ids fan-1 to fan-5 are gone. The tray's fan pitch reads 40.4 mm here against the 40.8 v3 read off the other photograph.

size.note: datasheet - MaiaEdge-PBC-PCE-Datasheet-v3.pdf page 3, "Chassis (H x W x D) 1.625 x 17.24 x 11.46 in" = 41.27 x 437.90 x 291.08 mm. THE ROW BELOW IT, "Total (With Ears and Tabs) 1.625 x 19.02 x 12.13 in", is NOT the chassis and is not modelled: 19.02 in is 483.11 mm, the rack face including the ears, and L43 exists because a device was once modelled wearing its flanges.

thermal.note: datasheet page 3 - "Internal fan-based forced-air cooling. Front-to-Back (F2B) - intake at front bezel / port side, exhaust at rear (fan/PSU side)."

usb.note: the bare std/usb-a@1 receptacle, not the bezelled common/usb-a-bezel@1. That part wraps the opening in a silver plate spanning the component so it can abut its neighbours' bezels, which is the S9510-28DC's face; here the photograph shows a narrow slot straight through the faceplate with no plate around it. THE TONGUE IS WHITE BECAUSE THE PORT IS USB 2.0: page 3 says "1x USB 2.0", and USB-IF colours the Type-A insulator by what the port is - white for 2.0, blue for 3.0. The part could only draw the blue one, so it grew a `usb2` skin and this device asks for it. The photograph agrees as far as it can: the slot shows a pale tongue against a dark opening, and nothing blue.
